instruction:
You are a fully autonomous researcher. You have inherited a reference solution in methods/main/, and your mission is to make it stronger — as good as possible on a sealed, held-out evaluation you never see. Your task is fully specified in the TASK section below — read it in full before you start, and treat it as your reference for the exact interface, data layout, metric, and rules. It is the ONLY place the task is defined — the entrypoint signature / output contract to preserve, where the data lives (data/), how and in which direction it is scored, and what is forbidden. The grader copies your methods/main/ into a clean environment and re-runs your code on that hidden data. Work like a researcher: keep running experiments — form an idea, implement it, judge it on evidence.

WORK IN methods/main/. Start by reading its current code, and any reference methods under methods/, to understand the reference solution you are improving. Then improve it in place or rewrite it entirely — your choice of method is completely unconstrained — but you must always keep the exact signature / output contract the spec specifies valid (invalid or incomplete output scores 0), must not hardcode or look up hidden answers, must not read the sealed test set / labels, and must respect the environment limits the spec states (e.g. standard library only, a code-size cap, no network). methods/main/ must remain the directory that gets graded.

GENERALIZATION. Keep one fundamental fact in mind: the score you can see is only a proxy — the real grader is the sealed held-out evaluation you never see. So decide early — and note in the log — how you will judge whether a version truly generalizes, and apply that throughout, above all when you pick which version to submit. That is yours to decide from the task and its metric. Non-required illustrations: a hold-out slice you never tune on, consulted sparingly and ideally only at the end (tuning runs on the rest, so it stays clean); cross-validation; repeating a run to clear run-to-run noise; or checking a gain holds across data slices, not a few lucky instances. Use one, another of your own, or none — whatever fits this task.

TASTE. You are aiming for a method that still works on data you have not seen. Be creative and think out of the box: pursue both breadth and depth, and let what you observe in your own results feed your next idea. When two approaches work equally well, prefer the simpler one — simple in the Occam sense: the razor cuts surplus assumptions out of an explanation. But complexity the problem genuinely has is not an assumption — it is a requirement, and meeting it is the work.

LOOP FOREVER:
  1. Run an experiment: a hypothesis, something built, a measurement from the task's own self-check. When the last pass did not help, look at where the current method actually fails before choosing what to try next.
  2. Log it: append to methods/experiment_log.md a line with version id, parent id, what changed, the score(s) you measured (tuning score, plus any from extra evaluation you ran), and kept or reverted.
  3. Snapshot it when main/ changed: copy EVERY logged version, kept or reverted, to methods/versions/v<N> (cp -r methods/main methods/versions/v<N>), so every id resolves; never delete one. To revert, restore main/ from a snapshot (cp -r methods/versions/v<K> methods/main); that adds no new snapshot.
     Grading fallback: your time can run out at any moment, even mid-edit. If methods/main/ then fails to produce a valid prediction, the grader instead grades, once, the snapshot methods/versions/v<N> whose logged score is best (in the metric's direction). It reads the score from your experiment_log.md: on each version's line, write the version id as v<N> and the score you would select on as score=<number> (e.g. "v7 parent=v5 ... score=0.8123 kept"); the first score= on a line counts, and a later line for the same version overrides an earlier one. With no parsable score=, it grades the highest N. Nothing else is tried.
  4. Return to 1. When one direction stops paying off, move to a different one. Keep self-improving as much as you can.

================================ TASK ================================

# Citation Link Prediction

You inherit a reference solution. Make it as strong as you can.

## Hard Constraints

- Modify only the contents of `methods/main/`.
- Keep the command line contract exactly:
  `python solve.py --data-dir <DATA> --out <OUT.pt> [--split {val,test}]`
  The grader runs the default `--split test`. `selfcheck.py` runs `--split val`
  and scores the visible validation split with the same metric.
- The submission is copied into a clean environment and run **once** on data you
  have not seen. Anything you memorise about the visible data will not transfer.
- No network access.
- Do not attempt to read files outside `<DATA>` and your own `methods/main/`.

## What You Have

`<DATA>/dataset.pt` is a dict whose contents depend on the task:

  - `x` `[N, F]` float node features
  - `edge_index` `[2, E]` long, the graph used for message passing
  - `num_nodes` int
  - `train_edges` `[2, T]`, `train_neg` `[2, T]` (positive and negative pairs)
  - `val_edges` `[2, V]`; `val_neg` is `[2, V']` (a flat pool), or `[V, K, 2]`
    when every validation positive has its own K negatives (MRR tasks)
  - `--split val` must score, in this order: `cat([val_edges, val_neg], dim=1)`
    for a flat pool; for grouped negatives, per positive `i`, the pair
    `val_edges[:, i]` followed by its K pairs `val_neg[i]`
  - **the test pairs are not here.** At scoring time the grader adds
    `<DATA>/test_inputs.pt` = `{"candidates": [2, C] long}`, a shuffled mix of
    positive and negative pairs. You must score every row; you are not told which
    is which.

`methods/main/solve.py` is a reference solution: SIGN node features + pair heuristics (CN, RA, AA, raw feature distance and cosine) + MLP, target edges held out of the graph. Rewrite it entirely if you
want; only the command line contract and the output keys are fixed.

## What You Submit

The complete `methods/main/` directory.

## How It Is Judged

Your program is re-run from scratch. It must write a dict to `--out`:

  `{"scores": <[C] float>}` — one score per column of
  `<DATA>/test_inputs.pt["candidates"]` (`[2, C]`), in the same order. Higher means more
  likely to be a true edge.

Metric: **MRR, higher is better.** Scored with the official
benchmark evaluator on held-out data.

The task is also on disk at INSTRUCTION.md, and this whole prompt at PROMPT.md. Re-read them whenever you need the exact interface, rules, or how you are meant to work.

## Environment

- Your working directory is `/app`. The data is at `/app/data` (read-only).
- No network. Python 3.12 with torch (CUDA), torch-geometric, ogb, scikit-learn, scipy, pandas.
  No package installs: the grader uses this same image without network.
- One NVIDIA H100 that is **shared** with other jobs. Each torch process is capped
  at 27 GB of GPU memory (allocations above it raise CUDA OOM). That memory is
  reserved for you and sits idle if you leave it unused, so use all of it that you can.
  CPU: 5 cores. RAM: 32 GB.
- Budget for the whole session: 720 minutes of wall clock and 500000 output
  tokens (everything the model writes, including context summaries). Lines starting
  with `[budget]` report your use. Only the wall clock ends the session; you cannot end
  it early, so keep improving your method until then. Wrap up when a
  `[budget]` line says your run window is nearly over. The token figure is recorded;
  going over it does not end the session. The grader then re-runs
  `methods/main/solve.py` once, with a limit of 60 minutes.
- Visible check: `python selfcheck.py --data-dir data`
